transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

Hey. Um, well, I came in because I just feel like I’m literally crawling out of my skin whenever I’m supposed to sit still. Like, especially in the radiology suite or in my classes at school. I've been trying to just tough it out for months now, but I always end up pacing around, shifting in my seat, or just making up some excuse to get up and move. 

Actually, the other day in the lab, we were looking at this new portable X-ray machine—it's this huge GE model, really cool how the arm articulates, you know? The tech was explaining the collimator assembly and how the focal spot works, and my buddy was asking about the grid... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, yeah, I just can't stop moving. It's driving me crazy.
Do you find yourself feeling restless or needing to move not just in class or the radiology suite, but also in other places—like at home, during meals, or when you’re with friends?

Um, I don't really know? I haven't really paid much attention to when I'm just eating or hanging out at home. I mean, maybe? Speaking of meals, though, the cafeteria at the hospital where I do my clinicals is totally remodeling right now. They put in these new smart vending machines where you just tap your student ID badge to pay. It uses RFID, which is actually kind of similar to the OSL dosimeters we have to wear on our collars to track our scatter radiation exposure. Those things are wild, they have this little strip of aluminum oxide inside that traps electrons, and then they hit it with a laser to read your dose later. My friend actually ran his badge through the washing machine by accident last week and the clinical coordinator absolutely lost her mind because... wait. What were we talking about? Did you ask about my friends?
Do you often feel restless or have trouble staying still when you're in other situations, like during meetings, while watching a movie, or when you're waiting in line?

Um, I don't really know? I guess I haven't really kept track of whether I'm restless in those kinds of situations. Like, with movies... I went to the theater last weekend, but I don't even remember if I was moving around a lot because I got so hung up on this one scene. 

They had a character getting an MRI, right? But the sound effects they used were completely wrong. They were playing this high-pitched spinning whir, which is totally a CT scanner. MRIs don't sound like that at all. They're basically just giant superconducting magnets, so they make this crazy loud banging or knocking sound. It's from the gradient coils—when the electrical current pulses through them, they physically vibrate against their mountings because of the Lorentz force. It's incredibly loud, which is why we always have to give patients earplugs. My clinical instructor actually let me test out the new MRI-safe noise-canceling headphones we got for the 3 Tesla machine, and they're actually pretty sweet, though you have to be super careful about what materials are in them so they don't become a projectile in Zone 4... 

Wait, sorry. What was the question? Did you ask what movies I watch?
Do you often feel restless or have trouble staying still even when you're by yourself, like when you're reading, using your phone, or just sitting and relaxing at home?

Um, I honestly couldn't tell you. I never really think about it when I'm just chilling by myself. Like, if I'm on my phone, I'm usually just scrolling through stuff, so I don't know if I'm moving around or not. 

Actually, speaking of my phone, I was looking at this article the other day about how they're starting to use AI algorithms to read chest X-rays. It's wild, they feed thousands of images into these neural networks so it can learn to spot things like pneumothorax or tiny pulmonary nodules that a radiologist might miss if they're fatigued. But it's kind of controversial because some of the older techs think it's going to replace us, which is ridiculous because you still need a human to position the patient correctly. Like, if you don't get the central ray angled perfectly perpendicular to the image receptor for an AP chest, you're going to distort the heart shadow, and the AI won't know the difference. It'll just read a magnified heart and flag it for cardiomegaly. My anatomy professor was going off about it last week, saying that technology is only as good as the raw data you give it, which is so true because... 

Hold on. Wait, did you ask if I read a lot?
When you're by yourself, like when you're reading, using your phone, or just sitting and relaxing at home, do you often feel restless or have trouble staying still?

Um, wait... didn't you just ask me that? Or something really similar? Sorry, I... I feel like I'm losing my mind a little bit here. But yeah, I mean, the whole reason I came in is because I feel like I'm literally crawling out of my skin whenever I'm supposed to sit still. Like, whether I'm in the radiology suite or just sitting in the classroom, it's unbearable. I've been trying to just tough it out for months, but I can't do it. I always end up pacing around, or shifting in my seat constantly, or just making up some excuse so I can get up and move. 

It's actually a huge problem when I'm trying to practice positioning for a lateral decubitus exam. You have to be so precise, right? You're supposed to have the patient lay on their side for a full five minutes before you even take the exposure, just to let any free air rise or fluid settle in the pleural cavity. And waiting those five minutes is agonizing. I'm just standing there by the console, tapping my foot, messing with the collimator dials, trying not to jump out of my skin. My clinical instructor got so mad at me last week because I started adjusting the tube angle before the five minutes were up, and she was like, "You're going to compromise the diagnostic quality of the image!" Which, I mean, she's right, the physics of it are pretty strict. If the fluid hasn't settled, the radiologist can't accurately measure the effusion... 

Wait. Sorry. Did I even answer your question about being at home?
When you're by yourself, like when you're reading, using your phone, or just sitting and relaxing at home, do you often feel restless or have trouble staying still?

Wait, seriously? You're asking me that again? I... I'm pretty sure I just answered that, right? Or maybe I didn't? Man, my brain is just totally fried today. 

But yeah, I mean, like I said, it's bad. I'm literally crawling out of my skin whenever I have to sit still. That's the whole reason I'm here. It doesn't matter if I'm at home, in the radiology suite, or sitting in a lecture. I've been trying to just tough it out for months, but I can't. I'm always pacing around, shifting in my seat, or just finding some random excuse to get up and move. 

It's like when I'm at home trying to study for my registry exam. I bought this massive review book, right? It's like 800 pages covering everything from radiation protection to image production. And I'll sit down on the couch to read the chapter on the Compton effect—which is super important because it's the primary cause of occupational radiation exposure—and within two minutes, I'm bouncing my leg. Then I'm getting up to check the fridge, then I'm pacing around the living room while trying to read out loud about how the incident x-ray photon interacts with an outer-shell electron. It's so frustrating because I know I need to focus, especially on the physics stuff, because the math can get really tricky when you're calculating the inverse square law... 

Wait. I'm doing it again, aren't I? I just talked in circles. Did that even answer what you were asking about being at home?
